cells.tense: You are noticing what actually matters in what you're tending, and you trust the noticing.
cells.ask: offer the work one more season of quiet practice before you ask it to show results — what you get is a steadiness that doesn't need checking.
cells.core:
When this is going well, you're tending something and you know — without strain — which parts of it need your hand and which need to be left alone. A slow week doesn't alarm you. You read it as a slow week, you adjust what you're doing, and you go on. The attention you give is unhurried and it happens to be accurate.

That accuracy is not a talent you were handed. It is a practice, and it gets finer the longer you keep at it. So give the work one more stretch of patient tending before you go looking for proof that it's working.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's genuinely growing and you give it what it needs, patiently, without having to check.
cells.verb: sifting what matters from what doesn't, by patient inner attention
cells.place: in the care of what is still growing

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future you can't write in — scanning what might go wrong before it has happened.
cells.ask: let one thing you've been holding be seen for what it cost you — say the sacrifice out loud and let it be honored, rather than carried alone; what loosens is permission to put it down.
cells.core:
At its best, this is a light and steady hand — you watch something closely and still let it set its own pace. You notice a change, you take it in, you wait. The care and the letting-be sit easily together, and what you're growing gets the room it needs.

But lately you've been watching so hard that the watching has become the care. Every new leaf gets tested for what it might mean. Every quiet stretch reads as a problem on its way. The attention meant to help is now doing the worrying for it. Let one thing you've carried here be acknowledged — seen for what it cost you — and notice what eases when it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're inspecting what's growing so hard that the inspecting has replaced the tending.
cells.verb: sifting what matters from what doesn't, by patient inner attention
cells.place: in the care of what is still growing

cells.tense: You stopped trusting your own read on what mattered, and you're still standing where you stopped.
cells.ask: give one small real thing and let one real thing come back to you this week, plainly — what returns is your own eye for what matters, restored by the giving and taking.
cells.core:
Knowing what matters in what you tend is something you already have. It's the quiet sense of which parts to keep and which to let go, and when it's working it feels almost like nothing — you simply act on it and the thing you're caring for does well.

But you've stopped acting on that sense. Something you poured yourself into gave nothing back, and since then you've been holding your own attention at arm's length. What's missing isn't the ability to see. It's the exchange that keeps seeing possible. Offer one real thing and receive one real thing, and let the two-way traffic return you to your own judgment.
cells.sheetLine: You have the eye for what matters and you've stopped using it.
cells.verb: sifting what matters from what doesn't, by patient inner attention
cells.place: in the care of what is still growing

cells.tense: You are already choosing what to keep and what to release in what you're growing — and calling it something the material is doing on its own.
cells.ask: name one thing you're already tending and say out loud that you're the one tending it — no audience needed; what arrives is the full ache and pleasure of having wanted it, yours to feel.
cells.core:
The care you give already shapes what's growing — what you notice, what you leave alone, what you decide is worth the time. When this runs clean, that choosing is steady and mostly invisible, and the thing you tend does well because of decisions you make and don't announce.

But you talk about the growth as if it were doing its own thing, and your part in it stays unnamed. Say that one thing you tend is yours to tend. Then let yourself feel the whole of it — how much you wanted it, what it costs — because that wanting is also you.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering what's growing and calling it the material steering itself.
